questions.question: Which table row gives the correct number of monosaccharides and disaccharides shown in the sweetness graph?
questions.answer: B: 2 monosaccharides and 3 disaccharides.
steps: The graph shows five sugars: lactose, maltose, glucose, sucrose and fructose.
Monosaccharides are single sugar units: glucose and fructose, so there are 2.
Disaccharides are two units joined together: lactose, maltose and sucrose, so there are 3.
Row B (2 and 3) is therefore correct.

questions.question: Which bond joins two monosaccharides together to form a disaccharide? A ester, B glycosidic, C hydrogen, D phosphodiester.
questions.answer: B glycosidic bond.
steps: A disaccharide is two monosaccharides joined together.
The link is a glycosidic bond, a C-O-C linkage formed between two sugar rings.
Ester bonds link fatty acids to glycerol, and phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides, so A and D are wrong.
Hydrogen bonds are weak and hold chains together rather than joining monomers, so C is wrong.

questions.question: State two conclusions about the relative sweetness of monosaccharides and of disaccharides from the graph.
questions.answer: Fructose is the sweetest sugar (1.75); monosaccharides are not all sweeter than disaccharides, e.g. sucrose (1.0) is sweeter than glucose (0.74).
steps: Read the bars: lactose 0.16, maltose 0.33, glucose 0.74, sucrose 1.0, fructose 1.75 (relative sweetness).
Conclusion 1: fructose, a monosaccharide, is the sweetest sugar shown, about 1.75 times as sweet as sucrose.
Conclusion 2: disaccharides vary widely in sweetness (0.16 to 1.0) and sucrose is sweeter than glucose, so being a monosaccharide does not guarantee more sweetness.
Alternative acceptable point: lactose is the least sweet sugar, and the two monosaccharides are on average sweeter than the three disaccharides.

questions.question: Devise an investigation a student could carry out to confirm the sweetness data shown in the graph.
questions.answer: Make equal-concentration solutions of each sugar and have a blind taste panel rank their sweetness, repeating for reliability.
steps: Prepare solutions of each monosaccharide and disaccharide at the same mass per volume (e.g. g per 100 cm3).
Keep temperature and volume of each sample the same so only the sugar type varies.
Use a blind taste panel, so the tasters do not know which sugar they are tasting.
Ask tasters to rank or score sweetness, because sweet taste comes from sugar binding to receptors on taste buds.
Repeat with several tasters and trials, then compare the mean scores with the graph.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structures of amylose and amylopectin, the two components of starch.
questions.answer: Both are polymers of alpha glucose; amylose is unbranched with 1-4 bonds and forms a helix, while amylopectin is branched with 1-4 and 1-6 bonds.
steps: Similarity: both are polysaccharides made of alpha glucose monomers joined by glycosidic bonds.
Similarity: both contain 1-4 glycosidic bonds in the main chain.
Contrast: amylose is an unbranched chain, so it coils into a compact helix.
Contrast: amylopectin has 1-6 glycosidic branches, which make it more open and branched.

questions.question: Which general formula is correct for a monosaccharide? A CnHnO2n, B CnH2nOn, C C2nHnOn, D C2nH2nOn.
questions.answer: B CnH2nOn.
steps: Monosaccharides have carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:2:1.
Glucose is C6H12O6, which fits CnH2nOn with n = 6.
A has too few hydrogen atoms, and C and D have twice as many carbons as oxygens, so they are wrong.
Glucose (C6H12O6) fits this formula with n = 6, confirming the general ratio.

questions.question: Name the reaction that joins two monosaccharides together to form a disaccharide.
questions.answer: Condensation reaction (with removal of water).
steps: Two monosaccharides are joined by a glycosidic bond.
A hydroxyl group from one sugar and a hydrogen from another are lost as water.
Joining molecules and releasing water is called a condensation reaction.
Water is released in the reaction, so it is a condensation reaction and not hydrolysis.

questions.question: Identify the carbohydrate described in part (i) of the diagram.
questions.answer: C: lactose.
steps: Lactose is the disaccharide found in cow's milk (glucose + galactose).
Amylose is a polysaccharide and galactose is a monosaccharide, so A and B are wrong.
Sucrose is a disaccharide but is the sugar found in plants such as sugar cane, not milk.

questions.question: Identify the carbohydrate described in part (ii) of the diagram.
questions.answer: C: maltose.
steps: The question sits on the disaccharide branch, so the answer must be a disaccharide.
Maltose is two alpha glucose units joined by a 1-4 glycosidic bond, so it contains only glucose.
Sucrose contains fructose, galactose is a monosaccharide, and amylopectin is a polysaccharide.

questions.question: Identify the carbohydrate described in part (iii) of the diagram.
questions.answer: C: glycogen.
steps: Glycogen is the polysaccharide used as the energy store in animals.
Amylose is the plant store, and fructose and sucrose are not polysaccharides.

questions.question: Identify the carbohydrate described in part (iv) of the diagram.
questions.answer: B: amylopectin.
steps: Amylopectin is a branched polysaccharide, with 1-6 glycosidic bonds at the branch points.
Amylose has only 1-4 bonds, and fructose and maltose are not polysaccharides.

questions.question: Draw a diagram of a water molecule to show its dipole nature.
questions.answer: A bent H2O: oxygen labelled delta-minus, each hydrogen labelled delta-plus, bond angle about 104.5 degrees.
steps: Draw one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms bonded to it at an angle of about 104.5 degrees, so the molecule is bent.
Label the oxygen with a partial negative charge (delta-minus), because oxygen is more electronegative and pulls the shared electrons toward it.
Label each hydrogen with a partial positive charge (delta-plus).
Optionally show the dipole arrow pointing toward the oxygen, showing the charge separation that makes water a polar solvent.

questions.question: Describe the effect of temperature on the solubility of salts F, G and H from the graph.
questions.answer: F: solubility rises steadily with temperature; G: rises sharply to 30 C then falls slowly; H: unaffected (constant at 30 g per 100 g water).
steps: Salt F: solubility increases in a straight line, from about 6 g at 0 C to about 78 g per 100 g water at 80 C.
Salt G: solubility increases steeply (curved) from about 5 g at 0 C to a maximum of 50 g at 30 C.
Salt G: above 30 C solubility decreases gradually, to about 40 g at 80 C.
Salt H: solubility stays constant at 30 g per 100 g water at all temperatures, so temperature has no effect.

questions.question: How many times more soluble is salt G than salt H at 30 C? Options: A 15.00, B 1.67, C 1.50, D 0.60.
steps: At 30 C salt G has a solubility of 50 g per 100 g water (its peak).
At 30 C salt H has a solubility of 30 g per 100 g water.
Ratio = 50 / 30 = 1.67, so salt G is 1.67 times more soluble than H.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the effect of temperature on the solubility of sodium chloride and glucose in water, using the graph.
questions.answer: Both are more soluble at higher temperature, but glucose is far more soluble and its solubility increases much more steeply than that of NaCl.
steps: Similarity: the solubility of both sodium chloride and glucose increases as temperature rises from 10 C to 60 C.
Difference: glucose rises from about 75 to about 300 g per 100 cm^3 (an increase of about 225), whereas NaCl rises only from about 45 to about 55 g (about 10).
Difference: the glucose curve gets steeper with temperature (non-linear), while NaCl is almost a flat straight line.
Glucose is more soluble than NaCl at every temperature shown.

questions.question: Using the table, calculate the molecular mass of glucose, given that the formula mass of sodium chloride is 58.44.
steps: Glucose is C6H12O6.
Carbon: 6 x 12 = 72.
Hydrogen: 12 x 1 = 12.
Oxygen: 6 x 16 = 96.
Molecular mass = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180.

questions.question: Calculate how many times greater the molecular mass of glucose is than the formula mass of sodium chloride.
questions.answer: 3.08 (3 significant figures)
steps: Ratio = molecular mass of glucose / formula mass of NaCl.
So glucose is 3.08 times greater (3 s.f.).

questions.question: Suggest why sodium chloride and glucose differ in solubility in water.
questions.answer: Glucose is more soluble because its many -OH groups hydrogen bond with water; NaCl is ionic and dissolves only as its ions are attracted to the charged ends of water molecules.
steps: Water is polar (O delta-, H delta+), so it can dissolve both polar molecules and ions.
Glucose has several polar -OH groups, which form many hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so large amounts dissolve.
NaCl is an ionic lattice: Na+ and Cl- have to be pulled out of the lattice by ion-dipole attraction to water, and the graph shows much less NaCl dissolves.
The difference in the type and number of attractions to water explains the difference in solubility.

questions.question: Explain why fatty acids are less soluble in blood than glucose and sodium chloride.
questions.answer: Fatty acids have long non-polar hydrocarbon tails that cannot form hydrogen bonds or ion-dipole interactions with water, whereas glucose and NaCl are polar or ionic.
steps: Blood is mainly water, which is a polar solvent.
Fatty acid tails are long hydrocarbon chains made of C-H bonds, which are non-polar.
Non-polar tails cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so they repel water and stay poorly dissolved.
Glucose has many polar -OH groups that form hydrogen bonds with water, and NaCl is ionic, so both dissolve well.

questions.question: Complete the description of water by writing the most appropriate word in each gap. Water has an uneven charge distribution so it is described as a ________ molecule. The hydrogen ends of the molecule have a very slightly ________ charge. Water is involved in the transport of substances so it is an important ________ in living organisms. Water is needed in chemical reactions called ________ reactions that break down disaccharides such as ________ into glucose and galactose.
questions.answer: Polar; positive; solvent; hydrolysis; lactose.
steps: Water has an uneven charge distribution (bent shape, O more electronegative), so it is a polar molecule.
The hydrogen ends have a slight positive charge (delta-plus), and the oxygen end is slightly negative.
Because it is polar it dissolves many substances, so water is an important solvent for transport.
Breaking a disaccharide by adding water is hydrolysis, which cleaves the glycosidic bond.
Lactose (glucose + galactose) is the disaccharide that breaks into glucose and galactose.

questions.question: How many of three statements about starch in living cells are correct: starch is a mixture of two polysaccharides; starch contains only 1-6 bonds; starch is insoluble in water? Options: A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: C two.
steps: Statement 1 is correct: starch is a mixture of amylose and amylopectin, two polysaccharides.
Statement 2 is wrong: starch has 1-4 bonds in its main chains, and only amylopectin also has 1-6 branch bonds.
Statement 3 is correct: starch granules are insoluble in water, so it can be stored without dissolving.
Two statements are correct, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Complete the description of disaccharides: the covalent link is a glycosidic bond; sucrose and lactose both contain glucose; sucrose also contains fructose; lactose also contains galactose.
questions.answer: Glycosidic; glucose; fructose; galactose.
steps: Two monosaccharides are joined by a covalent glycosidic bond.
Both sucrose and lactose contain one glucose unit.
Sucrose is glucose plus fructose.
Lactose is glucose plus galactose.

questions.question: Gentiobiose is formed from two identical monosaccharides. Name the reaction that joins them.
questions.answer: Condensation reaction.
steps: Two identical monosaccharides (glucose) are joined by a glycosidic bond.
Each join removes a molecule of water.
Joining molecules with loss of water is a condensation reaction.
The product is a disaccharide made of two glucose units, so the bond formed is a glycosidic bond.

questions.question: Each monosaccharide in gentiobiose has molecular mass 180. Which is the molecular mass of gentiobiose? Options: A 144, B 162, C 342, D 360.
steps: Two monosaccharides of mass 180 give a total of 2 x 180 = 360.
Forming one glycosidic bond by condensation removes one water molecule, mass 18.
Gentiobiose mass = 360 - 18 = 342, which is option C.
Gentiobiose is a disaccharide, so its molecular mass is the sum of the monosaccharide masses minus the water lost.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show a 1-2 glycosidic bond between glucose carbon 1 and fructose carbon 2.
questions.answer: Draw an oxygen atom as a bridge between C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose (C1-O-C2), with the OH groups on those carbons removed.
steps: A glycosidic bond is a C-O-C link between the two sugar rings.
Remove the OH from carbon 1 of glucose and the OH from carbon 2 of fructose (they leave as water).
Draw one oxygen atom bonded to carbon 1 of glucose and to carbon 2 of fructose.
Each C-O line must be a single bond joining the two ring structures.

questions.question: Complete the formula equation for the reaction that makes sucrose from glucose and fructose.
steps: Glucose and fructose are both C6H12O6.
Sucrose is C12H22O11 (C6H12O6 + C6H12O6 - H2O).
The glycosidic bond forms by condensation, so one water molecule is released.
Balancing: 2 C6H12O6 gives C12H22O11 + H2O.

questions.question: Give a reason why colour intensity is directly proportional to the concentration of sucrose.
questions.answer: The more sucrose present, the more coloured product is formed, so more light is absorbed and the colour is more intense.
steps: The test reagent reacts with sucrose (or its breakdown products) to form a coloured product.
Reagent is in excess, so the amount of coloured product depends on the amount of sucrose.
More coloured product absorbs more light, so intensity increases in proportion to concentration.
A higher concentration gives more coloured product, so absorbance rises in a straight line over the working range.

questions.question: Suggest why the calibration line does not start at the origin of the graph.
questions.answer: Some colour or absorbance is present even with no sucrose, from the reagents or water, so the line is offset from zero.
steps: A solution with zero sucrose should give zero colour, but the reagents may already be slightly coloured.
This background colour gives a reading above zero at zero concentration.
So the line shifts upward and does not pass through the origin.
A blank correction is needed to set the zero, because the offset shows background colour.

questions.question: State why the concentration of maltose and lactose cannot be measured using the sucrose test.
questions.answer: Maltose and lactose contain no fructose, so no coloured product forms with the chemical that binds fructose (and the enzyme is specific to sucrose).
steps: The test breaks sucrose into glucose and fructose, then adds a chemical that binds to fructose and changes colour.
Maltose is glucose + glucose and lactose is glucose + galactose, so neither releases any fructose.
Without fructose there is no colour change, so colour intensity cannot be used to measure their concentration.

questions.question: Put one cross in each row of a table to show whether each bond is present in amylose and amylopectin.
questions.answer: Glycosidic bonds: both amylose and amylopectin; 1-6 alpha bonds: amylopectin only; hydrogen bonds: both amylose and amylopectin.
steps: Both are polymers of alpha glucose joined by glycosidic bonds, so tick "both" in row 1.
1-6 alpha bonds form the branches, which only amylopectin has (amylose is unbranched with 1-4 bonds only), so tick "amylopectin only" in row 2.
Hydrogen bonds stabilise the coiled helix of amylose and the folded, branched structure of amylopectin, so tick "both" in row 3.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions about the effect of temperature and source of starch on the loss of amylose, from the graph.
questions.answer: 1: more amylose is lost as temperature rises (e.g. cassava 9% at 60 C to 94% at 80 C). 2: the source matters, cassava loses the most amylose and potato the least.
steps: Read the bars (% amylose lost at 60 / 70 / 80 C): potato 4 / 6 / 24; cassava 9 / 60 / 94; sweet potato 8 / 15 / 64; maize 8 / 25 / 58.
Effect of temperature: for every source, the higher the temperature the greater the % amylose lost, with the largest rise between 70 and 80 C.
Effect of source: at 70 C and 80 C cassava loses the most amylose (60% and 94%) and potato the least (6% and 24%).
At 60 C all four sources lose little amylose (4 to 9%), so the differences between sources are small.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the effects of temperature on the loss of amylose and amylopectin from rice, using the graph.
questions.answer: Both rise with temperature to a peak at 85 C then fall; amylopectin is lost from 20 C (amylose from 40 C), and above about 65 C more amylopectin than amylose is lost.
steps: Similarity: the concentration of both in the liquid increases as temperature rises, reaches a maximum at 85 C (amylopectin about 10.4 a.u., amylose about 5.2 a.u.) and then falls at 90 C.
Difference: amylopectin is detected from 20 C (about 0.6 a.u.), but no amylose is lost until 40 C (0 a.u.).
Difference: from about 45 to 65 C slightly more amylose than amylopectin is lost, but above about 65 C the loss of amylopectin is greater.
Difference: between 60 and 85 C amylopectin rises much more steeply (1.8 to 10.4 a.u.) than amylose (2.8 to 5.2 a.u.).

questions.question: Comment on the effect of the replacement liquids on the hardness and stickiness of cooked rice, using the table.
questions.answer: Amylose in the liquid makes rice harder (19.42 to 27.63) with almost no change in stickiness (1.19 to 1.21); amylopectin makes it stickier (1.19 to 1.71) with little change in hardness (19.42 to 20.43).
steps: Compare with the water control (hardness 19.42, stickiness 1.19).
Amylose: hardness increases by about 8.2 a.u. (to 27.63) but stickiness is almost unchanged (1.21), so amylose mainly increases hardness.
Amylopectin: stickiness increases by 0.52 (to 1.71) but hardness changes only slightly (20.43), so amylopectin mainly increases stickiness.
Both together give hardness 27.65 and stickiness 1.70, almost the same as amylose alone for hardness and amylopectin alone for stickiness, so the effects appear independent.

questions.question: Suggest why rice should be cooked in a measured volume of water, with the lid on, until all the liquid is absorbed, using the table.
questions.answer: So the amylose and amylopectin lost into the cooking liquid are reabsorbed and not poured away; liquid containing them gives harder and stickier rice (27.65 and 1.70) than water alone (19.42 and 1.19).
steps: Cooking releases amylose and amylopectin from the rice into the cooking water.
If all the liquid is absorbed (lid on, measured volume), these starch molecules go back into the rice rather than being lost.
The table shows liquid containing both increases hardness (19.42 to 27.65) and stickiness (1.19 to 1.70), so the rice keeps its intended texture.

questions.question: Draw a diagram of a water molecule to show its dipole nature.
questions.answer: A bent H2O: oxygen labelled delta-minus, each hydrogen labelled delta-plus, bond angle about 104.5 degrees.
steps: Draw one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms bonded to it at an angle of about 104.5 degrees, so the molecule is bent.
Label the oxygen with a partial negative charge (delta-minus), because oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself.
Label each hydrogen with a partial positive charge (delta-plus).
The uneven charge makes water a polar molecule, which is why it is a good solvent.

questions.question: Match each statement about carbohydrates to the correct carbohydrate by putting one cross in each row of a table.
questions.answer: Row 1 (general formula CnH2nOn): monosaccharides only. Row 2 (glycosidic bonds): polysaccharides only. Row 3 (little effect on water potential): polysaccharides only.
steps: Monosaccharides have the formula CnH2nOn; polysaccharides are made by condensation and lose water, so they do not fit this formula. Tick "monosaccharides only".
Glycosidic bonds join monosaccharide units together, so they occur in polysaccharides and not in single monosaccharides. Tick "polysaccharides only".
Polysaccharides are large and insoluble, so they have little effect on water potential; soluble monosaccharides lower it. Tick "polysaccharides only".

questions.question: What type of chemical reaction breaks a lactose molecule into two monosaccharides? A condensation, B esterification, C hydrogen bonding, D hydrolysis.
questions.answer: D hydrolysis.
steps: Breaking a disaccharide into two monosaccharides cleaves the glycosidic bond.
The bond is broken by adding a molecule of water.
Breaking a molecule by adding water is hydrolysis, so the answer is D.
Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation and is catalysed by enzymes such as lactase in the gut.

questions.question: Milk contains 4.9 g of lactose per 100 g. Each gram of lactose gives 16 kJ. Calculate the energy from the lactose in 200 g of milk.
steps: Lactose in 200 g of milk = 4.9 g x (200 / 100) = 9.8 g.
Energy = 9.8 g x 16 kJ per g.
Check: 100 g gives 4.9 g, so 200 g gives double, 9.8 g, which is sensible.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structures of glycogen and starch, the carbohydrate energy stores.
questions.answer: Both are polymers of alpha glucose with 1-4 bonds and 1-6 branches; glycogen is more highly branched and more compact than starch.
steps: Similarity: both are polymers of alpha glucose joined by 1-4 glycosidic bonds.
Similarity: both have 1-6 glycosidic branch points.
Contrast: glycogen has more frequent branches (about every 8-12 glucose units), which allows faster release of glucose.
Contrast: glycogen is more compact, while starch (amylose and amylopectin) is less branched.

questions.question: State one difference between the structure of a saturated lipid and an unsaturated lipid.
questions.answer: An unsaturated lipid has at least one C=C double bond in its fatty acid chain; a saturated lipid has only single C-C bonds.
steps: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds in the hydrocarbon chain.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds.
The double bonds cause kinks, which change how the molecules pack together.
Unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature because kinks prevent tight packing.

questions.question: Describe how a triglyceride is synthesised.
questions.answer: Glycerol combines with three fatty acids by condensation reactions, forming three ester bonds and releasing three water molecules.
steps: A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules.
Each fatty acid carboxyl (COOH) group reacts with a hydroxyl (OH) group on glycerol.
Each reaction is a condensation that removes one water molecule and forms an ester bond.
Three condensation reactions give one triglyceride and three water molecules.

questions.question: Which pair of elements is found in all amino acids? A carbon and oxygen, B carbon and sulfur, C nitrogen and magnesium, D oxygen and magnesium.
questions.answer: A carbon and oxygen.
steps: All amino acids contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
Sulfur is only in some amino acids (e.g. cysteine), so B is wrong.
Magnesium is not part of amino acids, so C and D are wrong.
Carbon and oxygen are present in every amino acid, so A is correct.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes how two amino acids are joined together in an enzyme molecule?
questions.answer: C: peptide, condensation.
steps: Amino acids are joined by a peptide bond (CO-NH), so A and B (ester) are wrong.
The bond forms when a molecule of water is removed, which is a condensation reaction, not hydrolysis.
Row C (peptide, condensation) is correct.

questions.question: Describe how a chain of amino acids can form an enzyme molecule.
questions.answer: The polypeptide chain folds into a specific 3D shape (tertiary structure), held by bonds between R groups, which forms the active site.
steps: Amino acids join by peptide bonds (condensation) to form a polypeptide chain.
The sequence of R groups determines how the chain folds.
Hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic interactions between R groups hold the chain in a specific 3D shape.
This shape creates an active site with a complementary shape to the substrate, so the enzyme works as a catalyst.

questions.question: Complete the account of the primary structure of a protein: amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, formed between the amino group of one and the carboxyl group of the next by a condensation reaction, during translation.
questions.answer: Peptide; amino; carboxyl; condensation; translation.
steps: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
A peptide bond forms between the amino (NH2) group of one amino acid and the carboxyl (COOH) group of the next.
The bond forms by a condensation reaction, releasing a molecule of water.
The chain is built on the ribosome during translation, which is the stage of protein synthesis where the bonds are made.

questions.question: Using the table, state which type of bonding is true for the secondary and tertiary structures of a protein.
questions.answer: Secondary structure: hydrogen bonds only. Three-dimensional structure: both hydrogen and ionic bonds.
steps: The secondary structure (alpha helix or beta pleated sheet) is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups only.
The three-dimensional (tertiary) structure is held by hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds between R groups (as well as disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions).
So tick "hydrogen bonds only" for secondary and "both hydrogen and ionic bonds" for 3-D structure.

questions.question: Describe two structural features of insoluble fibrous proteins such as keratin.
questions.answer: Long polypeptide chains lying parallel to form strands, with a regular repeating sequence of amino acids and cross-links that give strength.
steps: Fibrous proteins consist of long, parallel polypeptide chains that form strands or sheets.
They have a regular, repeating sequence of a few amino acids, so the chains pack together closely.
Cross-links such as hydrogen bonds or disulfide bridges hold the chains together, giving strength.
Their shape is not globular, so the molecules are insoluble in water.

questions.question: Draw the complete structure of the amino acid cysteine, given its R group.
questions.answer: A central alpha carbon bonded to H, an amino group (NH2), a carboxyl group (COOH) and the R group -CH2-SH.
steps: Every amino acid has a central alpha carbon bonded to a hydrogen atom.
The alpha carbon is also bonded to an amino group (-NH2) and a carboxyl group (-COOH).
The fourth bond is to the R group, which for cysteine is -CH2-SH (a thiol group).
The thiol -SH groups of two cysteines can form a disulfide bridge (S-S), which cross-links keratin.

questions.question: Describe the secondary structure of a polypeptide.
questions.answer: The polypeptide chain folds into a regular shape, either an alpha helix or a beta pleated sheet, held in place by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of the backbone.
steps: Secondary structure is the local folding of the polypeptide backbone.
The two common forms are the alpha helix (a coil) and the beta pleated sheet (folded strands).
Hydrogen bonds form between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N-H group of another.
These hydrogen bonds hold the regular shape in place.

questions.question: Explain the results of the investigation into the effect of two temperatures on the lengths of the primary and secondary structures of a polypeptide, using the table.
questions.answer: The primary structure stays 505 nm because strong peptide bonds are not broken at 55 C; the secondary structure lengthens (48 to 70 nm) because heat breaks its weak hydrogen bonds.
steps: Primary structure length is 505 nm at both 25 C and 55 C: it is held by strong covalent peptide bonds, which are not broken at 55 C.
Secondary structure increases from 48 nm to 70 nm (an increase of 22 nm, about 46%).
It is held by weak hydrogen bonds, which are broken or stretched as the molecules gain kinetic energy and vibrate more at 55 C.
The helix or pleated sheet therefore partly unwinds, so the structure becomes longer.

questions.question: Which statements about water are correct? 1 H2O is joined by hydrogen bonds; 2 water is a solvent; 3 oxygen has a small negative charge and hydrogens small positive charges. Options: A 1 and 2, B 1 and 3, C 2 and 3, D 1, 2 and 3.
questions.answer: C 2 and 3 only.
steps: Statement 1 is wrong: the oxygen and hydrogen atoms in a water molecule are joined by covalent bonds, not hydrogen bonds (hydrogen bonds link molecules).
Statement 2 is correct: water is a polar solvent.
Statement 3 is correct: the uneven charge distribution makes oxygen slightly negative and hydrogen slightly positive.
So statements 2 and 3 are correct, answer C.

questions.question: Put one cross in each row of a table to show whether each structure is present in amylose and amylopectin.
questions.answer: Glycosidic bonds: both; 1-4 alpha bonds: both; branched side chains: amylopectin only.
steps: Both amylose and amylopectin are alpha glucose polymers joined by glycosidic bonds, so tick "both".
1-4 alpha glycosidic bonds form the main chains in both molecules, so tick "both".
Branched side chains (from 1-6 bonds) occur only in amylopectin; amylose is unbranched, so tick "amylopectin only".

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show a peptide bond joining the two amino acids shown.
questions.answer: The carboxyl C of the first amino acid bonds to the amino N of the second, forming -CO-NH- and releasing one water molecule.
steps: Identify the COOH group on the first amino acid and the NH2 group on the second.
Join the carbon of the COOH to the nitrogen of the NH2 with a single C-N bond.
Remove the OH from the COOH and one H from the NH2, which form a water molecule.
The bond formed is a peptide bond (-CO-NH-), made by condensation.

questions.question: Suggest why the insects were removed from the galls before the investigation into protein and amino acid concentrations.
questions.answer: The insects contain their own proteins and amino acids and respire, so leaving them in would change the results for the gall tissue.
steps: The investigation measures the protein and amino acids in the plant tissue of the gall.
Insects are living organisms with their own proteins and amino acids.
If they stayed in the sample, their own molecules would be measured too.
Removing them ensures the results show only the plant gall tissue.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes the solubility of alanine, aspartate and tryptophan in a non-polar organic solvent, given their R groups in a diagram?
questions.answer: B: alanine, tryptophan, aspartate (most to least soluble).
steps: A non-polar solvent dissolves non-polar R groups best and charged R groups worst.
Alanine (CH3) is small and non-polar, so it is the most soluble.
Tryptophan has a large ring and hydrocarbon group that is mostly non-polar, so it is moderately soluble.
Aspartate has a charged carboxylate group (COO-), so it is the least soluble; this matches row B.

questions.question: Calculate how many times more soluble histidine (43.5 g per dm3) is than leucine, given the mass of leucine that dissolves in 250 cm3 of the same solvent.
questions.answer: 1.98 (about 2 times)
steps: Convert leucine to g per dm^3: 5.5 g in 250 cm^3 = 5.5 x (1000 / 250) = 22 g dm^-3.
Histidine is 43.5 g dm^-3.
Ratio = 43.5 / 22 = 1.977..., so histidine is 1.98 times more soluble (3 s.f.).

questions.question: Explain the results showing protein and amino acid concentrations in healthy leaf tissue, leaf tissue with galls and galls, using both graphs and the table of five amino acids.
questions.answer: Galls contain far more protein (24 vs 5 mg per g) and amino acids (39 vs 21 mg per g) than healthy leaf, because the insect saliva enzymes change the plant tissue so nutrients build up in the galls to feed the larva.
steps: Protein: 5 mg per g in healthy leaf, 13 in leaf with galls and 24 in galls, so galls have about 5 times more protein than healthy tissue.
Amino acids: 21 in healthy leaf, 24 in leaf with galls and 39 in galls, so galls have about 1.9 times more amino acids; amino acids are the monomers used to build the extra protein.
Saliva enzymes change the nutrients in the leaf and cause the plant to concentrate or synthesise protein and amino acids in the galls, giving the developing insect a rich food supply.
Table: histidine is absent from healthy and galled leaf tissue but abundant (++) in galls, so it is made or accumulated only in the galls.
Arginine (and alanine) fall in leaf with galls but are most abundant in galls, suggesting they are transported from the rest of the leaf into the galls.
Leucine stays the same (+) everywhere and tryptophan is absent everywhere, so not all amino acids are affected; the effect is selective.
